title: Amazon Just Raised Its India Bet to $48 Billion. The AI Data Centres Come First.
excerpt: CEO Andy Jassy met PM Modi in New Delhi and unveiled $13 billion in fresh cloud and AI spending — the latest salvo in a hyperscaler arms race that is reshaping India's digital economy.
body:
Andy Jassy arrived in New Delhi on Thursday with a number that landed harder than any pitch deck: $13 billion in fresh capital for AI and cloud infrastructure, stacked on top of the $35 billion Amazon committed just six months ago. The company's total planned investment in India between 2026 and 2030 now stands at $48 billion — and its cumulative spending since entering the country in 2010 will exceed $88 billion by decade's end.

The announcement came after Jassy met Prime Minister Narendra Modi, their third face-to-face since 2023. "We've been serving customers, sellers, developers, startups, and enterprises in India for more than a decade and just getting started," Jassy wrote on X after the meeting.

The new money has a clear destination: AWS data centres in Mumbai and Hyderabad, the twin poles of India's cloud computing ecosystem. The expansion will give Indian startups, enterprises, and government agencies access to Amazon's custom Trainium AI chips, managed AI services through Bedrock, and the full stack of developer tools that power Silicon Valley's generative AI boom. In total, more than $21 billion of Amazon's India commitment is earmarked for AI and cloud infrastructure alone.


![Prime Minister Narendra Modi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5f/The_official_portrait_of_Shri_Narendra_Modi%2C_the_Prime_Minister_of_the_Republic_of_India.jpg)


## The Hyperscaler Arms Race



> **""We've been serving customers, sellers, developers, startups, and enterprises in India for more than a decade and just getting started," Jassy wrote on X after the meeting."**


Amazon is not investing in a vacuum. India has become the most contested AI infrastructure market outside the United States and China. Google announced a $15 billion data centre commitment in October, targeting southern India. Microsoft earmarked $17.5 billion in December. Domestic conglomerates Reliance and Adani have made their own multi-billion-dollar plays.

What sets Amazon's approach apart is the sheer breadth of its India footprint. The company has already digitised 12 million small businesses, enabled $20 billion in cumulative e-commerce exports, and trained 10 million Indians in cloud skills. By 2030, it aims to support 3.8 million jobs — up from 2.8 million today — and push cumulative exports to $80 billion.


![Silicon Valley — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Silicon_Valley%2C_facing_southward_towards_Downtown_San_Jose%2C_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg/3840px-Silicon_Valley%2C_facing_southward_towards_Downtown_San_Jose%2C_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg)


Jassy also spotlighted Amazon Now, the quick-commerce service first incubated in India and now being replicated globally. Orders have doubled every quarter since launch, making it the fastest-growing business unit in Amazon India's history, with plans to scale to more than 300 cities this year.

## Why New Delhi Is Rolling Out the Carpet

India's eagerness to court hyperscalers is not just about jobs or foreign direct investment. It is about data sovereignty. With AWS's India Regions, customers can keep data within the country while accessing frontier AI tooling — a policy priority as New Delhi pushes for the kind of compute capacity it needs to run sovereign large language models, power digital public infrastructure, and build an AI ecosystem that is not wholly dependent on models controlled from San Francisco.


![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)


The government has sweetened the deal: long-term tax breaks for global cloud providers running India-based data centres for international workloads, part of a broader policy framework introduced earlier this year to attract exactly the kind of capital Amazon is now deploying.

## The Diaspora Connection

For the estimated 4.5 million Indian-origin professionals working in tech globally — many of them inside Amazon and AWS — the investment signals something deeper than infrastructure expansion. Indian-founded startups in the US and UK increasingly need AWS presence in India for latency-sensitive applications, data localisation compliance, and serving India's 800-million-plus internet users. Every new availability zone in Mumbai and Hyderabad reduces the friction for diaspora-led ventures building for both markets simultaneously.

The $48 billion figure also arrives at a politically useful moment. India and the US are negotiating a trade deal that both sides describe as "very close." A CEO-level investment announcement timed to a Modi meeting gives both governments something to point to as proof that the economic relationship is deepening even as tariffs and visa policies remain contentious.

*Sources: Reuters, TechCrunch, Barron's, Inc42, The Bridge Chronicle*
